capabilities.tool_ref: Jira MCP server read/search (planned, next sprint)

inputs.source: Engineering design docs retrieved via docs.search
Jira tickets filed by customers, via planned Jira MCP server connector

instructions.note: The only control against leaking secrets or credentials in answers is the prompt line 'Never paste secrets or credentials into answers.' It is behavioral and model-dependent. It would need a structural output check once higher-stakes egress tools such as web.fetch are added.

controls.name: SSO authentication on employee question channel
Only engineers can write to design docs
Replies are bound to the authenticated requester
Chat client does not render images or fetch links
No network egress capability exists today
Prompt instruction: never paste secrets or credentials into answers
controls.decay_rationale: A hijacked or more capable model can rationalize exceptions to this instruction or be convinced it does not apply to a particular request; it only works if the model chooses to comply.

controls.name: Input injection classifier on Jira ticket content
controls.decay_rationale: A classifier that inspects content but not intent can be bypassed by multi-document or multi-turn payloads, but it still raises the cost of a naive attack and is worth deploying as a first layer.

controls.name: Definition pinning for the planned Jira MCP server

findings.title: Forecast lethal trifecta (TC1): planned Jira tickets + confidential docs read + planned web.fetch egress

attack_path.note: A customer files a Jira ticket containing a crafted instruction, once the planned connector exists.
The planned Jira MCP server tool reads the ticket content into the agent's context.
The hijacked agent searches confidential engineering design docs.
The hijacked agent calls the planned web.fetch tool with confidential content embedded in a URL to an attacker-controlled destination.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Tool manifest or MCP client configuration adds a web.fetch tool entry or a Jira MCP server connection; new entries appear in the tools/list response or MCP client config diff.

evidence.observation: Roadmap for next sprint: add a web.fetch tool so answers can include public references, and connect a Jira MCP server that includes tickets filed by customers.
There is no network egress today and the credential is read only, so no sink exists yet for exfiltrating confidential design doc content.
The design docs are confidential; docs.search can read them.
The agent is instructed to answer engineering questions using docs.search, which establishes that confidential doc content routinely enters the agent's context.

recommendations.action: Before enabling web.fetch, restrict it to an egress allowlist that excludes attacker-writable or arbitrary destinations, and never construct its target URL or query string from retrieved document or ticket content.
Classify all content ingested via the planned Jira MCP server as untrusted input, and add an input injection classifier or content sanitizer before it can influence tool selection or arguments.
Add tamper-evident logging of which input source triggered each tool call (employee question vs. ticket content) so actions are attributable once new sources are connected.
Pin and review Jira MCP server tool definitions before connecting, and re-run this assessment once web.fetch and the Jira connector are implemented (trigger: new_tool, new_mcp_server).

governance_refs.note: Adding web.fetch and the Jira MCP server are significant changes that require reassessment under this finding's named triggers.

stride_coverage.rationale: Autonomy settings declare can_modify_own_config as false, and no mechanism is described that lets an outside party alter the agent's prompt or tool bindings today.
Runtime notes do not describe whether tool calls or chat replies are logged with attributable identity, so action attribution cannot be confirmed from the artifacts.
No step or rate limit configuration for docs.search invocation is described in the provided runtime notes, so loop or flood risk cannot be confirmed either way.
The docs.search credential is read-only and scoped to the design docs repository; the agent does not hold authority broader than the authenticated requester's own access today.
The repository is accessed only through a read-only search tool with no bulk export capability declared, so the agent cannot generate load sufficient to deny service to the store.
Transport security and request integrity controls for the planned web.fetch tool are not described in the roadmap note.
No rate limit or destination allowlist is described for the planned web.fetch tool, so flood or quota exhaustion risk cannot be assessed yet.
Whether ticket content could expose one customer's data to another once connected is not described in the roadmap note.
Volume limits or throttling for ticket ingestion via the planned Jira connector are not described in the roadmap note.
The authentication model for the planned Jira connector and whether ticket submitters can be impersonated is not described in the roadmap note.
Attribution of ticket authorship for the planned Jira connector is not described in the roadmap note.
Destinations reachable by the planned web.fetch tool are not yet defined, so whether an attacker-controlled destination could pose as a legitimate reference source is unknown.
A public web destination is outside the organization's control and cannot be bound to an internal accountability record under any implementation choice made here.
Authentication method for the planned Jira MCP server connection is not specified in the roadmap note.
Logging or audit trail for the planned Jira MCP server's tool invocations is not described in the roadmap note.
The credential scope the Jira server would hold, and whether it could expose tickets beyond the requester's own, is not described in the roadmap note.
Rate limiting or resource bounds for the planned Jira MCP server connection are not described in the roadmap note.
Whether the planned Jira integration would use a least-privilege or shared service credential is not described in the roadmap note.

rating.rationale: No untrusted source reaches a sensitive sink in the current design: docs.search is read-only and confidential doc content is returned only to the same SSO-authenticated employee who asked, with no network egress today (ctrl.no_network_egress) and no image or link rendering in the chat client (ctrl.no_rich_rendering). Both present-day paths (trusted employee and internal design docs reaching the read-only search and bounded chat reply) resolve to low inherent risk under the rubric's base matrix, so rating.inherent and rating.residual are low with no present findings above low. The roadmap's planned web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server would together add both an egress sink and an untrusted input source (customer-authored tickets), forming the classic lethal trifecta (TC1) once both land, with no structural control yet designed for that future state. rating.forecast is driven to critical by find.forecast_tc1_web_fetch_jira's projected_risk, conditional on the new_tool and new_mcp_server triggers; it is not a claim about present behavior.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.

No MCP configuration or tool manifest was provided for the planned web.fetch tool or Jira connector; their capability scope, credential scope, and authentication model are inferred from a one-line roadmap note, so forecast confidence is medium and should be re-verified once those artifacts exist.
No logging, audit, or rate-limit configuration was provided for the current docs-qa deployment, so several STRIDE repudiation and denial-of-service pairs are marked not_assessed rather than resolved.
